content:
Yesterday brought two contradictory reports about next year's iPhone model, the one tipped to be the 20th anniversary device and embody Apple's long-standing 'a single slab of glass' vision.

There have been conflicting reports for some time now about what we can actually expect, but yesterday's divergence was arguably the most dramatic yet…

The current situation

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has frequently talked about his long-term vision of eventually turning the iPhone into 'a single slab of glass'; even though Ive has departed, it's still generally believed that Apple is moving in that direction.

While Apple doesn't generally do big anniversary celebrations, the consensus is that they want to get as close to achieving that vision in time for the 20th anniversary of the iPhone. That likely includes embedding Face ID under the display, and hiding the front-facing camera under the display too.

However, we've already seen conflicting reports about these expectations. Originally the view was that this would be a standalone model, similar to an iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but more recent reports say the design will appear on the iPhone Pro models next year.

In sequence, that would be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple could also choose to skip a generation and name it the iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary.

Yesterday's contradictory reports

Yesterday's situation was further confused by an analyst claiming that Apple has abandoned the idea of an all-glass iPhone next year.

But Bloomberg's Mark Gurman immediately pushed back on that claim.

The more likely reality

The point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone doesn't have a single end point. What they plan to deliver next year is just one step, or a few steps, toward the sci-fi vision of 'a single slab of glass'.

The question is not whether this goal can be achieved next year, but how far Apple will move in that direction. But whether one step or several, this certainly won't be the final step in iPhone design evolution.

In fact, Gurman revealed that Apple has actually stepped back from its previously anticipated targets for next year.

The Jefferies analyst likely received the same information, just a beat later, and mistook it for the entire plan being shelved.

My personal expectation is that next year's design will be a big leap — comparable to the iPhone X breakthrough — but with more to come in the years that follow. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have a big enough breakthrough to warrant some kind of special branding, like labelling it as a 20th anniversary iPhone edition (which I think is unlikely), giving it a different special name, or skipping a generation to call it the iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Share them in the comments.
